result.topic_en: Euler treats the singular case in which both X and Y are perfect squares, perturbing them by an infinitely small quantity α so that √X = R + α/2R and √Y = S + α/2S, and begins re-evaluating Lagrange's integral form in terms of p = x + y.

§. 60. Statuamus igitur
$X=(a+bx+cxx)^2+\alpha$ et $Y=(a+by+cyy)^2+\alpha$,
ita vt pro litteris maiuſculis A, B, C, D, E, fiat $A=aa+\alpha$,
$B=2ab$, $C=2ac+bb$, $D=2bc$, $E=cc$, vbi $\alpha$
denotat quantitatem infinite paruam, deinceps nihilo aequa-
lem ponendam. Hinc ergo ſi br. gr. ponamus
$a+bx+cxx=R$ et $a+by+cyy=S$ erit
$\sqrt{X}=R+\frac{\alpha}{2R}$ et $\sqrt{Y}=S+\frac{\alpha}{2S}$.

§. 61. Nunc igitur conſideremus formam integra-
lis primo inuentam, quae erat
$\frac{\sqrt{X}-\sqrt{Y}}{x-y}=\sqrt{(\Delta+D(x+y)+E(x+y)^2)}$
pro qua igitur habebimus
$\sqrt{X}-\sqrt{Y}=R-S-\frac{\alpha(R-S)}{2RS}$.
Quia vero hic erit
$R-S=b(x-y)+c(xx-yy)$ fiet $\frac{R-S}{x-y}=b+c(x+y)$.

items.english: To resolve this one must therefore resort to a similar device, whereby the formulas X and Y are assumed not equal to the squares themselves but to differ from them infinitely little.
